profile.feeling: Size and importance: a big house, a big city — and, for people, being older.

senses.def: old, grown-up (of a person; often كَبِيرٌ فِي السِّنِّ)

examples.tr: My grandfather is old (advanced in years).
My brother is older than me.

phrases.meaning: the takbīr — said in the call to prayer and in moments of awe or joy

synonyms.nuance: great, mighty — greatness and importance rather than size

etymology.text: Adjective of the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) of the root ك ب ر (k b r), whose verb كَبُرَ means “to be or become big, to grow up” — inherited from Proto-Semitic *kabar-, with Hebrew כָּבַר (“to be great”); elative أَكْبَر (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its elative أَكْبَر is in the call to prayer: اللّٰهُ أَكْبَرُ, “God is greatest”.
Greek μεγάλος and German groß do the same double job: a big house, and an older person (ο μεγάλος μου αδελφός, mein großer Bruder = أَخِي الْأَكْبَرُ).
pitfalls: Plural for people: the broken plural كِبَار (الْأَوْلَادُ كِبَارٌ); plural for things: the feminine singular (الْبُيُوتُ كَبِيرَةٌ).
For age, كَبِيرٌ alone can be unclear: say كَبِيرٌ فِي السِّنِّ, or use مُسِنّ.
subtleties: أَكْبَرُ مِنِّي is both “bigger than me” and “older than me” — the context decides.

profile.feeling: Little things and little children.

examples.tr: The house is small but beautiful.
The little children are in the park.

synonyms.nuance: tiny, slight — amounts, chances, a small role

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from Proto-Semitic *ṣaɣir- (“to be small, young”); cognate with Akkadian ṣeḫrum (“small, young”) and Biblical Hebrew צָעִיר (ṣɔʿir).

funFacts: Hebrew צָעִיר (tsa’ir), “young”, is its cousin (Wiktionary).
Like كَبِير for “older”, صَغِير doubles as “younger”: أُخْتِي الصُّغْرَى = my youngest sister.
pitfalls: Plural for people: صِغَار (الْأَطْفَالُ صِغَارٌ); for things the feminine singular (الْغُرَفُ صَغِيرَةٌ).
صَغِير is “young” for children only; a young adult is شَابّ.
subtleties: أَصْغَرُ مِنِّي = smaller or younger than me; with family words it is almost always “younger”.

profile.feeling: Length in space and in time — a long street, a long wait — and a tall person.

senses.def: long (length; a road, hair, a text)

examples.tr: My father is a tall man.

synonyms.nuance: long, extended — mostly of time: عُمْرٌ مَدِيدٌ, a long life (in good wishes)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: a late adjective of the type CaCīC from the root ط و ل (ṭ w l) — an ancient word would have become *طَيِّل, like جَيِّد; ultimately from Proto-Afroasiatic *ṭVwl- (“long, far”).

funFacts: One word for long and tall, like Turkish uzun (uzun yol, uzun boylu); Greek, German and Russian split them (μακρύς / ψηλός, lang / groß, длинный / высокий).
طَاوِلَة (table) comes from Italian tavola; Wiktionary suggests it was reshaped to sound like a word of the root ط و ل — a table is “a long thing”.
pitfalls: Plural for people طِوَال (also طَوِيلُون); for things the feminine singular: الشَّوَارِعُ طَوِيلَةٌ.
For buildings and mountains Arabic prefers عَالٍ (high): بِنَايَةٌ عَالِيَةٌ; طَوِيل is above all for people and lengths.
subtleties: The question “how tall are you?” is about length: كَمْ طُولُكَ؟ — طُول (length, height) is the noun of the same root.

profile.feeling: Short things, short people, a short visit.

examples.tr: My brother is short and I am tall.

synonyms.nuance: brief, concise — texts and periods: بَعْدَ وَقْتٍ وَجِيزٍ, shortly after

etymology.text: Adjective of the root ق ص ر (q ṣ r); Wiktionary: cognate with Hebrew קצר (katsár, “short”) and Amharic አጭር (ač̣ər, “short”).

funFacts: Hebrew קָצָר (katsar) is the same Semitic word.
pitfalls: Plural for people قِصَار (also قَصِيرُون); for things the feminine singular.
قِصَّة (story) only looks similar: its root is ق ص ص.
subtleties: “Short of …, lacking” is not قَصِير but نَاقِص.

profile.feeling: Quality you can count on: a good book, good food, good work.

senses.def: “good” as a school mark (between مَقْبُول and مُمْتَاز)

synonyms.nuance: good, fine, nice — also of conduct; حَسَنًا = all right, OK
good, kind; tasty — warmer, for people and food

etymology.text: Wiktionary: an adjective of the type CaCīC of the root ج و د (j w d), from *جَوِيد (*jawīd) through *جَيِيد to جَيِّد; the w shows in the elative أَجْوَد.

funFacts: Arab school reports grade in words: مَقْبُول (pass), جَيِّد (good), جَيِّد جِدًّا (very good), مُمْتَاز (excellent).
Its root ج و د also gives جَوْدَة, quality.
pitfalls: “Better” is not formed from it in everyday Arabic: say أَفْضَلُ (or أَحْسَنُ) — هٰذَا أَفْضَلُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ.
“I’m fine” is أَنَا بِخَيْرٍ (lesson 2), not أَنَا جَيِّدٌ.
subtleties: جَيِّد is good in quality; for a good person طَيِّب or حَسَن sound warmer.

profile.feeling: Disappointment: bad food, bad news, bad luck.

examples.tr: He is not a bad man.

synonyms.nuance: poor, bad in quality — goods, food, work

etymology.text: Adjective of the root س و ء (s w ʾ), “to be bad”; the w of the root comes back in the elative أَسْوَأ, worse (Wiktionary).

funFacts: As a noun, سَيِّئَة is a bad deed — the opposite of حَسَنَة, a good deed.
pitfalls: The hamza sits on a yāʾ: سَيِّئ, سَيِّئَة, سَيِّئًا (also printed سيء).
“Worse” is أَسْوَأُ, with the w of the root: الطَّقْسُ الْيَوْمَ أَسْوَأُ.
subtleties: For food that has gone off, Arabic says فَاسِد (spoilt), not سَيِّئ.

profile.feeling: The pleasure of something new: a new car, a new phone, new students.

synonyms.nuance: modern, recent — حَدِيث is new in time, up to date

etymology.text: Adjective of the root ج د د (j d d), with the verb جَدَّ, “to be new” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same letters ج د د spell جَدّ, grandfather — a different word of the same written root.
pitfalls: Plural for people جُدُد (طُلَّابٌ جُدُدٌ); for things the feminine singular: الْكُتُبُ جَدِيدَةٌ.
“Newer, newest” is usually أَحْدَثُ (from حَدِيث), not the rare أَجَدُّ.
subtleties: مِنْ جَدِيدٍ (anew) is a fixed phrase: the adjective is used as a noun.

profile.feeling: Things with a past: an old house, the old town, an old friend.

examples.tr: This is an old car, but it is good.

synonyms.nuance: old, aged, antique — often with respect: an old house, a vintage piece

etymology.text: Adjective of the root ق د م (q d m), whose verb قَدُمَ means “to be old, to be ancient”; elative أَقْدَم (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The root ق د م also gives قَدَم (foot) and تَقَدَّمَ (to advance) — the idea of what goes before.
Many Arab cities have a الْمَدِينَةُ الْقَدِيمَةُ, the old walled town: Damascus, Jerusalem, Fez.
pitfalls: Not for the age of people: an old man is رَجُلٌ مُسِنٌّ (or كَبِيرٌ فِي السِّنِّ); رَجُلٌ قَدِيمٌ sounds odd.
Plural for people قُدَامَى (former, old: أَصْدِقَاءُ قُدَامَى) or قُدَمَاء (the ancients); for things the feminine singular.
subtleties: أَقْدَمُ = older (of things), the oldest: أَقْدَمُ جَامِعَةٍ فِي الْعَالَمِ.

override.pos: Wiktionary files شَابّ only as a noun (“young man, youth”); it is also the everyday adjective “young” (رَجُلٌ شَابٌّ, امْرَأَةٌ شَابَّةٌ), and its masculine forms here are those of Wiktionary’s noun table.

profile.feeling: Youth and energy: a young teacher, young people.

senses.def: young (of a person, from the teens to about thirty)
a young man (as a noun); الشَّبَاب = young people, youth

examples.tr: He is a tall young man.

synonyms.nuance: young in years — also for children

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of شَبَّ (šabba, “to become a young man, to grow up”).

funFacts: يَا شَبَاب! (“young people!”) is the everyday “guys!” of many dialects.
pitfalls: Not for small children: a young child is طِفْلٌ صَغِيرٌ.
The double b stays in every form: شَابٌّ, شَابَّةٌ, الشَّابُّ.
subtleties: Plural for people: شُبَّان (young men) or شَبَاب, which usually means “youth, young people” as a group.

profile.feeling: Respect for age: the polite word for elderly people.

senses.def: old, elderly, aged (of people) — the polite standard word

examples.tr: My grandfather is an elderly man.
My grandmother is old, but she is active.
My mother works in an old people’s home.

synonyms.nuance: old, “big in age” — the most common polite phrase
an old man, an old woman — mostly a noun, and blunt; it can sound disrespectful
an old man, an elder — respectful; also a title (sheikh)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of أَسَنَّ (ʾasanna, “to age”); compare سِنّ (sinn, “tooth, age”).

funFacts: سِنّ means both “tooth” and “age”: كَبِيرٌ فِي السِّنِّ is “big in age”, and مَا سِنُّكَ؟ asks “how old are you?”.
pitfalls: Politeness: about people say مُسِنّ or كَبِيرٌ فِي السِّنِّ; عَجُوز can be rude; never قَدِيم, which is for things.
The double n: مُسِنٌّ, مُسِنَّةٌ, مُسِنُّونَ.
subtleties: Everyday speech prefers كَبِيرٌ فِي السِّنِّ or simply كَبِيرٌ; مُسِنّ is the neutral word of news and institutions.

profile.feeling: Heat in the air — and on the tongue.

synonyms.nuance: hot to the touch — drinks, food, water

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of حَرَّ (ḥarra, “to be hot”); compare Hebrew חָרִיף (kharif, “sharp, spicy”).

funFacts: Its noun حَرَارَة (heat, temperature) went into Turkish as hararet (heat, fever, thirst).
pitfalls: Hot tea, coffee or soup is normally سَاخِن; with food حَارّ usually means SPICY: طَعَامٌ حَارٌّ.
The double r: حَارٌّ, حَارَّةٌ; the elative is أَحَرُّ (hotter).
subtleties: “It is hot” has no “it is”: الْجَوُّ حَارٌّ — the weather (is) hot.

profile.feeling: A steaming cup, hot soup, hot water.

senses.def: hot (to the touch: drinks, food, water, objects)
hot, tense (news, places): مَنَاطِقُ سَاخِنَةٌ, hot spots

examples.tr: The child has a temperature today.

synonyms.nuance: hot — weather and climate; spicy food

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of سَخَنَ / سَخِنَ / سَخُنَ (“to be or become hot”).

funFacts: In Egyptian and Levantine Arabic سُخْن (sukhn) is the everyday word for hot.
pitfalls: سَاخِن is for things you touch, eat or drink; for the weather say حَارّ: الْجَوُّ حَارٌّ.
subtleties: Drinks: شَايٌ سَاخِنٌ (hot tea) / عَصِيرٌ بَارِدٌ (a cold juice) — the classic café pair.

profile.feeling: Cold water, cold winters, cold drinks in the heat.

senses.def: dull, flat, unfunny (a joke, a person)

synonyms.nuance: feeling cold (of a person): أَنَا بَرْدَانُ, I’m cold

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of بَرَدَ (barada, “to be cold, to freeze”); cognate with Amharic ብርድ (bɨrd, cold).

funFacts: In the Qurʾān the fire is told to be بَرْدًا وَسَلَامًا, “coolness and peace”, for Abraham (21:69) — in hot lands coolness is a blessing.
pitfalls: “I’m cold” is not أَنَا بَارِدٌ (that sounds like “I’m a cold, dull person”): say أَشْعُرُ بِالْبَرْدِ (I feel cold), colloquially أَنَا بَرْدَانُ.
subtleties: Weather: الْجَوُّ بَارِدٌ (it is cold) — a sentence with no verb.

profile.feeling: Comfort: a warm room, warm milk, a warm spring day.

examples.tr: I drink warm milk before sleeping.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of دَفِئَ / دَفُؤَ (“to be warm”).

funFacts: Its root gives دِفْء (warmth) and مِدْفَأَة (a heater, a stove).
pitfalls: The hamza sits on a yāʾ in every form: دَافِئٌ, دَافِئَةٌ, دَافِئًا.
“I feel warm” is أَشْعُرُ بِالدِّفْءِ, not أَنَا دَافِئٌ.
subtleties: Things in the plural agree in the feminine singular: مَلَابِسُ دَافِئَةٌ (warm clothes).

profile.feeling: Beauty everywhere: a beautiful garden, a lovely day, a nice idea.

phrases.meaning: repaying a favour (الْجَمِيل here is a noun: a good deed)

synonyms.nuance: sweet, pretty, nice — the everyday word in many dialects

etymology.text: Adjective of the root ج م ل (j m l), whose noun جَمَال is “beauty”; elative أَجْمَل (Wiktionary).

funFacts: مَا أَجْمَلَ …! is the Arabic exclamation “how beautiful …!” — the elative with -a after مَا.
The camel, جَمَل, is written with the same root letters ج م ل; Greek κάμηλος and English camel come from the Semitic word.
pitfalls: For a man, وَسِيم (handsome) is the usual compliment; جَمِيل is said of women, things and places.
subtleties: As a noun, الْجَمِيل is a favour, a good deed: لَنْ أَنْسَى جَمِيلَكَ, I won’t forget your kindness.

profile.feeling: A strong word: ugly to look at, or shameful.

etymology.text: Adjective of the root ق ب ح (q b ḥ), whose noun قُبْح is “ugliness”; elative أَقْبَح (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Islamic theology debated الْحُسْن وَالْقُبْح, “the beautiful and the ugly” — whether good and evil can be known by reason.
pitfalls: About a person’s looks it is rude; speakers soften it: لَيْسَ جَمِيلًا (not beautiful).
subtleties: Often moral rather than visual: فِعْلٌ قَبِيحٌ, a shameful deed.

profile.feeling: Relief: an easy question, an easy way.

senses.def: flat, level (land); as a noun: a plain

phrases.meaning: Welcome! — you have come to your people and to easy, level land

etymology.text: Adjective of the root س ه ل (s h l), with the verb سَهُلَ, “to be easy”; elative أَسْهَل (Wiktionary).

funFacts: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا, the great Arabic welcome, contains it: “(you have come to) family and level ground”.
pitfalls: “Easily” is بِسُهُولَةٍ, not سَهْلًا.
Things in the plural: الْأَسْئِلَةُ سَهْلَةٌ (feminine singular).
subtleties: “It is easy to …” = مِنَ السَّهْلِ أَنْ … — the adjective is used as a noun.

profile.feeling: Effort: hard work, hard questions, hard times.

examples.tr: Arabic is hard, but it is beautiful.

phrases.meaning: difficult to deal with, stubborn (of a person)

etymology.text: Adjective of the root ص ع ب (ṣ ʿ b), with the verb صَعُبَ, “to be hard, difficult” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its plural صِعَاب is mostly used as a noun, “difficulties”: تَغَلَّبَ عَلَى الصِّعَابِ, he overcame the difficulties.
pitfalls: Things in the plural: الْأَسْئِلَةُ صَعْبَةٌ (feminine singular).
subtleties: “It is hard for me” = هٰذَا صَعْبٌ عَلَيَّ — with عَلَى.

profile.feeling: A bargain at the market.

examples.tr: This restaurant is cheap and good.
Vegetables are cheap at the market.

synonyms.nuance: low, modest — prices and sums: بِمَبْلَغٍ زَهِيدٍ

etymology.text: Wiktionary: an adjective of the pattern فَعِيل from the verb رَخُصَ (“to be cheap”); cognate with Amharic ርካሽ (rɨkaš, “cheap”).

funFacts: Amharic ርካሽ (rɨkaš) is the same Semitic word (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: About a person or behaviour it is an insult (cheap, base) — use it for prices.
subtleties: At the market: هَلْ عِنْدَكَ شَيْءٌ أَرْخَصُ؟ — do you have something cheaper?

profile.feeling: High prices — and people who are dear to us.

examples.tr: I don’t eat in expensive restaurants.

synonyms.nuance: precious, valuable — worth a lot, not just pricey
costly — of an activity: السَّفَرُ مُكْلِفٌ

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of غَلَا (ġalā, “to be excessive, to be or become expensive”).

funFacts: Wiktionary also gives it the sense “boiling” (the verb غَلَى is “to boil”): prices that boil over.
Its elative أَغْلَى never changes its ending: هٰذَا أَغْلَى مِنْ ذٰلِكَ.
pitfalls: A defective adjective: غَالٍ (nominative and genitive without al-), غَالِيًا (accusative), الْغَالِي (with al-); the feminine غَالِيَةٌ is regular.
In speech you hear غَالِي everywhere; in careful writing it is غَالٍ.
subtleties: يَا غَالِي (my dear) is a warm way to address a friend in many dialects.

profile.feeling: Joy and good luck: a happy holiday, happy people.

examples.tr: I’m happy to meet you. (a woman speaking)

synonyms.nuance: glad, delighted — the joy of the moment

etymology.text: Wiktionary: an adjective of the pattern فَعِيل from the verb سَعِدَ (saʿida, “to become happy”).

funFacts: The Romans called Yemen Arabia Felix, “happy Arabia” — in Arabic الْيَمَنُ السَّعِيدُ.
سَعِيد (Saeed) and سَعِيدَة are common names.
pitfalls: Plural for people سُعَدَاءُ — a diptote, no tanwīn: نَحْنُ سُعَدَاءُ.
subtleties: سَعِيد is lasting happiness and luck; فَرْحَان is joy at a moment.

profile.feeling: Sadness: a sad face, a sad song, a sad story.

etymology.text: Adjective of the root ح ز ن (ḥ z n); Wiktionary: the verb حَزِنَ, “to be or become sad, to grieve”, and the noun حُزْن, “sadness”.

funFacts: عَامُ الْحُزْنِ, “the Year of Sorrow”, is the year the Prophet Muḥammad lost his wife Khadīja and his uncle Abū Ṭālib.
pitfalls: Several plurals exist for people (حَزِينُونَ, حُزَنَاءُ, حَزَانَى); حَزِينُونَ is the safest.
Things in the plural: الْأَغَانِي حَزِينَةٌ (feminine singular).
subtleties: “Sad about” = حَزِينٌ عَلَى …; “it makes me sad” = يُحْزِنُنِي.

profile.feeling: The end of a long day.

examples.tr: We are tired; we want to sleep.

synonyms.nuance: tired — the everyday word in speech (also heard in standard Arabic)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the passive participle of أَتْعَبَ (ʾatʿaba, “to tire”), the form IV causative of تَعِبَ (taʿiba, “to be tired”) — literally “made tired”.

funFacts: Greek has the same pair: κουρασμένος (tired) / κουραστικός (tiring); Arabic changes one vowel: مُتْعَب / مُتْعِب.
pitfalls: مُتْعَب (mutʿab) = tired, مُتْعِب (mutʿib) = tiring: أَنَا مُتْعَبٌ لِأَنَّ الْعَمَلَ مُتْعِبٌ.
subtleties: In speech تَعْبَان is far more common; مُتْعَب is the standard written word.

profile.feeling: An empty stomach before dinner.

synonyms.nuance: hungry — the everyday form in speech (pattern فَعْلَان, like عَطْشَان)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: derived from the active participle of جَاعَ (jāʿa, “to become hungry”).

funFacts: A common saying: الْجُوعُ كَافِرٌ — “hunger is an unbeliever”: a hungry person respects no rules.
pitfalls: The hamza on a yāʾ: جَائِعٌ, جَائِعَةٌ.
Plural for people: جِيَاع (or جَائِعُونَ).
subtleties: “I am hungry” needs no verb: أَنَا جَائِعٌ — and a woman says أَنَا جَائِعَةٌ.

profile.feeling: A dry throat on a hot day.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: from عَطِشَ (ʿaṭiša, “to thirst”) + ـَان (-ān), of the root ع ط ش.

funFacts: The pattern فَعْلَان is the “state” pattern: جَوْعَان (hungry), عَطْشَان (thirsty), شَبْعَان (full), تَعْبَان (tired), زَعْلَان (upset).
pitfalls: A diptote: no tanwīn — أَنَا عَطْشَانُ, not عَطْشَانٌ.
The feminine is عَطْشَى in careful Arabic; عَطْشَانَة is everyday speech and common in modern writing.
subtleties: Plural for people: عِطَاش, for men and women alike.

profile.feeling: Speed: fast trains, fast food.

examples.tr: We ate at a fast-food restaurant.

etymology.text: Adjective of the root س ر ع (s r ʿ), with the verb سَرُعَ, “to be quick, to hurry” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Its noun سُرْعَة is “speed”: بِسُرْعَةٍ! = quickly! hurry up!
pitfalls: “Quickly” is بِسُرْعَةٍ (or سَرِيعًا).
subtleties: Faster = أَسْرَعُ: الْقِطَارُ أَسْرَعُ مِنَ الْحَافِلَةِ.

profile.feeling: Slowness: a slow bus, a slow walk.

examples.tr: The tortoise is a slow animal.

phrases.text: فِي التَّأَنِّي السَّلَامَةُ وَفِي الْعَجَلَةِ النَّدَامَةُ
phrases.tr: in slowness is safety, in haste is regret

etymology.text: Adjective of the root ب ط ء (b ṭ ʾ); Wiktionary: the verb بَطُؤَ, “to be or become slow, late”.

funFacts: اِمْشِ بِبُطْءٍ! (walk slowly!) uses its noun بُطْء.
pitfalls: The hamza changes its seat: بَطِيءٌ, but بَطِيئَةٌ and بَطِيئًا (on a yāʾ).
subtleties: Slower = أَبْطَأُ: الْحَافِلَةُ أَبْطَأُ مِنَ الْقِطَارِ.
